attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. The cited WSJ excerpt is the source he points to, but the assertion is his.

semantics.note: A retrospective observation about why Altman was fired in 2023. 'Appeared' is an evidential qualifier, but 'does in fact' makes the assertion firm. It is not a probabilistic hedge. The normalisation keeps the qualifier.

contract.note: Reading 'for lying' as the board's perceived dishonesty being a material reason is the ordinary reading of 'appeared to have gotten fired for lying'. It does not require proof of deliberate lies. That is fair and not stretched. The result depends on this reading, as the contract flags.

evidence.note: Dated 2023-11-17. The board's own announcement ties the removal to Altman being 'not consistently candid' with the board. This is the dismissing body's stated reason, so it is direct evidence of motive, not self-praise.

Firsthand account from Toner, a director who voted for dismissal, published May 2024. She says Altman withheld information and misrepresented things, in some cases outright lying to the board, and gives this as the background to the firing.

OpenAI's summary of the WilmerHale review (March 2024). It says the November post accurately stated the board's rationale and cites a loss of trust. It also says his conduct did not mandate removal. That limits any claim of proven lies but does not deny perceived dishonesty as the motive.

reviews.rationale: The board's contemporaneous statement gives a lack of candour as the reason for the removal. Toner, a director who voted for it, later described outright lying. The WilmerHale summary confirms that statement accurately gave the board's rationale. Its finding that removal was not mandated concerns whether the firing was justified, not the board's motive. So the qualified claim that Altman appeared to be fired for lying is supported under the contract's fair reading.
